{{DISPLAYTITLE:The second theorem, and why it is not the first}}

''Mathematical counterpart: [[Noether's theorems/Second theorem/The second theorem stated and proved|The second theorem stated and proved]].''

[[File:NT-F-13.png|thumb|right|360px|alt=Two groups of five bars representing field equations. On the left, without a local symmetry, all five are independent. On the right, one free function makes the fifth follow from the other four, shown by a curved arrow. A caption states the counting: one arbitrary function gives one identity and one equation that was never independent.|Identities among the field equations from a local symmetry]]

If you already know the first theorem, the hardest thing about the second is
unlearning the shape of the first.

== The statement ==

Take a scoring rule for whole histories. Suppose it survives a symmetry you can
dial differently at every point, of the kind on
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/Symmetry that can differ from place to place|the
previous page]]. Count the free shapes.

Then for each free shape there is a '''relation among the equations of motion
themselves''' — a statement that certain combinations of them, and of their rates
of change, add up to exactly nothing.

Read that twice. Not a flowing quantity. Not a total that stays put. A statement
that the equations are tied to each other.

== Nine tenths of the proof is shared ==

Here is the part that is genuinely surprising, and it is worth knowing before you
read either proof.

The two theorems are proved from the same place. Everything — the scoring rule,
the nudge, the careful business about
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/What happens at the edges|which thermometer you
are reading]], the loss of the integral sign — is common to both. Both proofs
arrive at a single relation and then stop being the same proof.

They part at exactly one step.

== The one step ==

Suppose the symmetry is global — one knob, one number, the same everywhere.

Then the relation you have arrived at is a sum of independent pieces, one per
knob, and independent pieces can be separated. Turn one knob and hold the others
still, and only that piece can be responding. Do it for each knob and the single
relation falls apart into one relation per knob. Those are the first theorem's
conserved flows.

Now suppose the symmetry is local — a free shape.

You cannot do that. The pieces are not independent. Your free shape appears in the
relation, and so does the rate at which your shape varies from place to place, and
those two are not separate things you can hold still against one another. Choose
the shape and you have chosen how it varies. There is nothing to pull apart.

So the proof has to do something else, in two moves.

'''First, trade.''' There is a standard manoeuvre for shifting a rate of change
off one factor and onto the other, at the cost of an extra term that only ever
contributes at the edges. Apply it repeatedly and the rates of change of your free
shape are gone. Only the shape itself is left, multiplied by something built out
of the equations of motion.

'''Second, choose.''' Now use the freedom. Pick a shape that is whatever you like
in the middle of some region and fades to nothing near its boundary. The
edge-terms all die, because there is nothing at the edges for them to be made of.
What survives is a total, over the region, of your arbitrary shape multiplied by
that combination of equations.

That total is zero, and it is zero for '''every''' shape you could have drawn. The
only way a quantity can be zero against every possible shape is by being zero
itself.

'''So the combination of equations is zero.''' Not flowing. Not conserved. Zero.

== Why you could not have done this with numbers ==

The second move is the whole difference. It needed a shape that is busy in the
middle and quiet at the edges.

A knob cannot do that. A knob is one number applying everywhere, and it cannot be
told to fade out near a boundary. This is why no amount of adding knobs to a
global symmetry ever produces this theorem, and it is the precise sense in which
the two theorems have different inputs rather than different amounts of the same
input.

== What it does not give you ==

'''No conserved quantity.''' There is no flow and no total. If you go looking for
the second theorem's conserved charge you will not find one, because there is not
one.

'''No dependence on physics.''' The relation holds whether or not anything is
obeying the equations of motion — it is a statement about the equations, not about
their solutions. What happens when you do impose them is a separate question with
a surprising answer, on
[[Noether's theorems/Explainers/Counting the equations a gauge theory really has|its
own page]].
